Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that put my body under stress

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something wrong with me as a person

issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, carrying a weapon is hard to reconcile clinically with the indexed trauma and the rest of the profile. It implies danger from interpersonal or environmental attack rather than illness-related threat, with no supporting triggers, memory, or appraisal content indicating assault-related fear.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: Scanning for exits and being unable to believe reassurance about safety can occur in severe PTSD, but together they suggest a persistent external attack/escape-based threat style that fits poorly with a life-threatening illness trauma unless there is clear accompanying illness-specific danger content. No such illness-linked threat items are present.

issues.item: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out
issues.explanation: The profile is clinically incoherent because it omits Triggers and Memory entirely despite an extreme PTSD severity (PCL-5=73) and instead concentrates on severe Threat, Negative Appraisals, and Maladaptive Strategies without any plausible illness-linked intrusion or cue structure.

issues.item: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Circumstances ... (eg, being in the dark)' is poorly matched to a life-threatening illness trauma and points toward an assault/accident-type fear context rather than medical trauma; this clashes with 'Avoid Medical Cues' which is the trauma-congruent avoidance item.

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: 'Dissociate Deliberately' is possible in PTSD, but paired here with strongly illness-specific avoidance and no memory/trigger content, it suggests a different symptom profile and lacks support from the stated formulation, which centers Threat–Appraisal–Strategy cycling rather than dissociative disengagement.

issues.item: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy item 'Avoid Circumstances ... (eg, being in the dark)' is not well aligned with the trauma type of life-threatening illness. The example implies a threat context more typical of assault/accident trauma, while the rest of the profile centers on medical cues.

issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Medical Cues' and 'Avoid Thinking' fit illness trauma, but 'Avoid Circumstances ... being in the dark' pulls toward a different trauma context, reducing within-node coherence.

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: Cross-node coherence is weakened because the threat items emphasize generalized danger and delays, while the negative appraisals are purely global self-defectiveness/weakness with no illness-related or health-related meaning. For life-threatening illness, some link is expected between medical threat and appraisals; these items instead suggest a different or more diffuse formulation.

vignette: Chung was a 35-year-old UX Designer with a South Eastern Asian background who had recently been struggling with intense psychological distress following his near-fatal battle with a serious illness. Married and devoted to his work, Chung’s trauma began when he faced life-threatening complications that left him feeling deeply vulnerable and afraid. Chung's traumatic experience led him to believe there was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person, an idea that only intensified his emotional numbness and sense of weakness. These negative appraisals made it difficult for him to engage in normal daily activities without feeling overwhelmed by fear and anxiety. He had come to avoid anything related to medical cues such as hospitals or ambulances and even physical examinations, which he found intensely distressing. Chung's belief that there was something inherently defective about himself led him to adopt maladaptive strategies like avoiding thoughts about the traumatic event entirely. He would distract himself with work tasks but often felt his body tense up in anticipation of potential danger. This constant state of alertness made it difficult for him to trust others when they assured him he was safe. Instead, delays in any situation—such as waiting for test results or even traffic delays—led him to assume the worst. As Chung’s negative appraisals deepened, so did his sense of threat and maladaptive coping mechanisms. He became hyper-vigilant about physical stressors at work, avoiding situations that might put his body under strain. His occupation as a UX Designer required long hours sitting in front of a computer, which he found increasingly stressful because he associated any discomfort with the possibility of another health crisis. The constant tension and heightened alertness also began to affect his relationships. Chung’s wife noticed him becoming more distant and withdrawn, often cancelling plans at the last minute out of fear that something bad would happen if they went out. This pattern of avoidance further reinforced his negative beliefs about himself, creating a vicious cycle where he was convinced his fears were justified. Chung had started to avoid medical appointments altogether, which made his wife even more concerned. He found it impossible to believe her reassurances and often felt that she didn’t understand the depth of his anxiety. His body remained on high alert, always ready for something bad to happen, no matter how irrational this seemed to others. The turning point came when Chung was unable to complete an important project at work due to a panic attack triggered by a minor delay in receiving necessary materials. This incident made him realize that his condition was affecting not just his personal life but also his professional success and reputation. He felt increasingly isolated, both from his colleagues and his family. Chung’s current state is one of intense fear and hopelessness. What frightened him most was the possibility of another health crisis without any control over it. Seeking help now seemed like a last resort to break this vicious cycle before it consumed him completely. While he hoped for relief from his constant anxiety, he also feared being seen as weak and vulnerable by those around him. The prospect of therapy felt daunting but necessary, a chance to reclaim some sense of normalcy in his life. Chung’s journey toward seeking help was marked by the realization that his fears and avoidance behaviors were not just symptoms but a cycle feeding on itself. He hoped for support and understanding from others so he could start to rebuild trust in himself and the world around him.
